item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Trollope: He knew he was right
item.description: TLDR in summary: Better than expected. Pages: 800+ Finally! I started HKHWR in early 2019, but life happened and back it went into my library. In the meantime, seven years passed and I became a rather sophisticated reader. And since I don’t like loose ends, I decided to finish it, once and for all. I say that phrase because back in 2019, I read all the way near the second half, but somehow I couldn’t go further.

item.title: Why keep writing
item.description: Francis Bacon’s chew-and-digest category of books can, upon reflection, be also extended to essays and shorter writings. If the writing is good, length doesn’t matter. It was this idea that came up from the bottom of my subconscious well just now, but I’m not sure what else will turn up, so let’s go rummaging. For starters, every now and then I happen to chance upon a very well-written writing, either an essay or a blog post, or even a paragraph (such as the ones found on Amazon when someone takes the trouble and time to review a book for our benefit–for which I am grateful), that I find either useful, or interesting, or mind-bending, even hilarious, or simply well-written, etc.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Trollope: The Eustace Diamonds
item.description: On a whim, I had bought several Penguin Classics editions of Anthony Trollope’s novels, but several years ago when I picked one randomly, I had chanced upon ‘He knew he was right’, and I confess that at roughly 800+ pages, it seemed kind of slow-moving. As you probably know, I (am proud to) have ADHD, so it’s really not easy to do anything– let alone read. But as those who know how ADHD really functions already realize, once we’re certain our energy is not wasted, we pour it all in–what is called hyperfocus in certain circles.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Matthew Lewis: The Monk
item.description: Despite the fact that Lewis’s work has been unfairly villified by readers with substandard comprehension and critical thinking skills, one day when I finally regained access to my Penguin Classics library (it’s a long story and I don’t care to mention it), I decided it was time I read it. As soon as I read the introduction, I realized the book and its author were presented in an overly negative light–perhaps unintentionally or even unconsciously.

item.title: ☆★★★★★★★★★ Lermontov: A Hero of Our Time
item.description: What a fantastic find! Lermontov is a poet at heart and his prose shows it. The story was unputdownable, but at the same time, made me imagine, think, and even learn some real-world wisdom. Though he claimed that he was not using himself in the protagonist, he was subtly using the protagonist to express his own opinions. I know this because some of the things his protagonist was saying or thinking were almost similar to some ideas I had been entertaining, ideas that you can’t have unless you think them over for a very long time, and in response to vagaries of the social environment.

item.title: I'm alive
item.description: Greetings, stranger. The last essay I wrote here on my site is dated March 2024. After nearly 20 months, I’m back. Because I’m alive. Alhamdulillah. Around March 2024, I developed a mysterious condition. I was playing basketball nearly every day. Then all of sudden, I was bedridden. We’ll not go into the specifics. Let it be sufficient to know that within two weeks, I felt I was not going to make it alive.

item.title: ☆★★★★★★★★★ Pushkin: Queen of Spades
item.description: 9/10 Pushkin doesn’t need an introduction even to English-reading audiences, because of how great of an artist he is. And although I have read his works in good English translations by Penguin, one has to sadly admit that a lot can be lost even in the best of translations. For one, even merely re-arranging words and meanings in a sentence can change its poetic aspect. There is an energy detected in ’never stop improving’ but none in the trite-sounding ‘always keep improving’.

item.title: ☆☆☆☆☆★★★★★ Radcliffe: The Italian
item.description: 5/10 In others, kinda meh, but better than a bad book. That really is not praise in my book. It’s just one star shy of becoming a bad book. Still, I give it five instead of four stars because the book is not boring, if you look at it from a story-telling angle. But any critic or critically-thinking reader worth their salt already knows that fiction is not ‘made up stories’, nor we read it for the story-telling value only.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ PKD: The Adjustment Team
item.description: It’s been a while. Out of pure randomness, I ran into PKD’s short story “The Adjustment Team” which was intriguing and interesting. The scenery was described quite artistically, and only some of the characters were properly described, such as the old man with ‘his faded blue eyes mild– a deep, ancient mildness that made the Clerk tremble even more’. I think this selective description was on purpose, to show relative importances in a social hierarchy.

item.title: The Advantages of ADHD
item.description: As an empath and a left-handed person who thinks he’s ADHD, I’ve come to a stage in my life now, that just looking at someone’s photo evokes feelings in my mind, that usually if not always, prove to be mostly accurate. Actually, I only became conscious or discovered the fact that I am an empath, in late 2022. But for nearly four decades, I’ve been aware of a sort of power in my mind, which both fascinated me and irritated those who had underestimated me.
